blocks.note: The hands of the bot, and the longest file here. Lines 3 and 4 are the design of the whole project in two sentences: every decision or calculation that code can do is taken away from the model, because a weak model gets dates, sums and filters wrong and code does not. The model only picks which tool to use.

"tool" wraps a plain function into something a model can call, and z is Zod, which validates the arguments before your code sees them. Then the storage functions from harness/dados.ts, the spreadsheet functions from planilha.ts, and the search plus the cost-benefit score from voos.ts.

One short line with a large consequence. Everything that leaves your Mac is reached through this object, so the exam in harness/avaliar.ts can replace both entries with fakes and never touch Google or your Drive. If the code called buscarVoos directly, testing without the network would be impossible, and that is the only reason this indirection exists.

The scratchpad that lives for exactly one tools step: everything searched and still valid, the flights not yet in a spreadsheet, the searches made in this request, what you wrote, and the conversation id. harness/agente.ts builds it before the loop and copies it back into the state afterwards, which is how tools can share work without touching the graph state directly.

Every tool below starts by pulling the scratchpad out of config, which is how harness/agente.ts smuggles it in. Line 31 caps a request at twelve searches, because a model stuck in a loop must not hammer Google.

A hand-written table from city name to airport codes, and the reason the model never has to know an airport code. Cities with several airports map to several codes, which is why São Paulo searches GRU, CGH and VCP in one request. Lines 46 to 50 are the aliases a weak model does not know: Cumbica is GRU, Galeão is GIG, Heathrow is LHR, plus city names in English, French, Italian and German. Every key is lower case and unaccented, which is what the next function produces.

NFD splits an accented letter into a letter plus an accent mark, the regex deletes the marks, then lower case and trim. "São Paulo" becomes "sao paulo", matching the table keys. It is used all over this file, for cities, classes, airlines and your own messages.

Normalise, strip a leading "aeroporto de/do/da", then look the name up. If that fails and the text is exactly three letters, accept it as a code and let Google judge it, which keeps airports outside the table reachable. Otherwise throw, and read that message carefully: it tells the model to pass a code and to ask rather than guess. Every error in this file is written as an instruction, because it goes straight back to the model as the tool's result.

Today's date, and the locale trick: "sv-SE" happens to format dates as YYYY-MM-DD, which is the format the whole project uses. The timeZone option pins it to São Paulo, so the date does not shift because of where the machine thinks it is.

The date vocabulary. Twelve rows of month names in Portuguese, English, Spanish, French, Italian and German, unaccented, so "december", "diciembre" and "dezember" all resolve to the same month. DIAS_DA_SEMANA are the matching keys with index 0 for Sunday, which lines up with getUTCDay, and NOMES_DOS_DIAS is the pretty version used when talking back.

The weekday name of a date. The "T00:00:00Z" matters: without it JavaScript reads the string in local time and the day can come out wrong by one, which is exactly the kind of silent error this file exists to prevent.
Adding days by adding milliseconds, then cutting the first ten characters off the ISO string. Doing it in UTC avoids every daylight-saving surprise.

Builds the date string with zero padding, then checks it survives a round trip through Date. That check is the point: JavaScript turns 30 February into 2 March without complaining, and here that silent correction is an error worth reporting.
A day and month with no year means this year if it has not passed yet, otherwise next year. It is why "12/12" said in December 2026 means 2026 and said in January 2027 means 2027.

Numbers written as words. The table covers one to twenty plus thirty, and trocarNumeros handles the two-word forms like "vinte e tres" first, then replaces any remaining word found in the table. So "doze de dezembro" becomes "12 de dezembro" before any parser runs, which means the parsers below only ever deal with digits.

Dates with a month name, in both orders: day first for "12 de dezembro" and "12. Dezember", month first for "December 12, 2026". The optional suffixes cover º, st, nd, rd and th. Line 127 looks the name up across all six languages, and a found month with a year builds that exact date while one without takes the next occurrence.

The function that turns human text into a date, and the order of the chain is the logic. First a full ISO date. Then day/month/year with any separator, where padStart(4, "20") turns "26" into "2026". Then day/month alone, resolved to the next occurrence.

The named days and the relative ones. Christmas Eve is tested before Christmas and "depois de amanha" before "amanha", because the shorter phrase is contained in the longer one and would win otherwise. That ordering is the whole trick of this block. Then today, "daqui a N dias", and finally a month name.
"dia 13" with no month: this month if the day has not passed, otherwise next month, with the December rollover to January of next year written out explicitly rather than left to arithmetic.

The last resort: a weekday name. The formula gives 1 to 7 days ahead, never 0, so "sexta" said on a Friday means the following Friday rather than today. If no weekday is found either, it throws an instruction to ask which day, which is the correct ending for text that contains no date at all.

The final check: a date in the past is refused with an instruction to warn and ask. Without it, "01/01" said in December would quietly resolve to a day that has gone, and Google would return nothing for a reason nobody could see.

The lock against an invented date, and one of the two most important checks in the file. A date is only accepted if the day number, or some time word, actually appears in something you wrote. Line 176 lists those words in both languages. Line 177 builds a regex for the bare day number with an optional leading zero. The shortcut comment on line 171 is honest about the hole it leaves: "2 adultos" counts as the day 2, so an invented date on the 2nd would slip through. It stays until the exam shows it matters.

The single sentence shape every flight is shown in, which is what the model reads and what the checker later matches against. The duration goes through horas from planilha.ts, and the comment records the real bug behind that: the model once turned "1000 min" into "10h", so the conversion is done by code before the model ever sees a number.
The leg label and the grouping. Map.groupBy is the standard library doing the work, keyed by that label, so every tool below can present results per leg without repeating the logic.

The code picks the winners so the model does not have to: cheapest, fastest, best value and most expensive. Line 202 also attaches the ten cheapest, and the comment gives the real failure behind it: without the list, the model claimed an airline "did not appear" when it simply had not won a category. Line 203 adds "there are N more, use filtrar_voos", which is how the model learns there is more without being shown all of it.

The same summary for every leg, joined. It is also what the emergency answer in harness/agente.ts pastes when the writer has failed, which is why this text has to read acceptably to a human and not only to a model.

The internal search. The key is the six parameters joined, and line 215 returns null when that exact search already happened in this request, because weak models repeat themselves constantly. Line 216 enforces the twelve-search cap with a message telling the model to answer with what it has rather than to try again.

The search itself goes through servicos, so the exam can fake it. Then the refresh rule in three lines: flights from the same leg are filtered out and replaced by the new ones, in both lists, so searching a leg twice leaves only the newer prices instead of two generations side by side.

Searching several airports and days. Line 229 refuses a search where an origin is also a destination. Then three nested loops, each iteration in its own try, which is what makes one broken airport harmless. A null result means it was a repeat, so line 237 pulls those flights back out of the scratchpad instead of searching again. Zero results becomes a "no flights found" note. A failure becomes a warning spelling out "A BUSCA FALHOU ... this does not mean there are no flights", and that exact phrase is what the writer's rule 3 and harness/verificador.ts both look for.

The date gate used by every tool that searches. It parses the date, refuses one you never mentioned, and then adds a second check: if your last message named a weekday, the resolved date has to fall on it. The error tells the model to pass the date through as written, like "próxima sexta", rather than computing it itself, which is the behaviour that makes the whole date system work.

The lock against an invented place. Resolve the text to codes, then find every table name pointing at those codes, so GRU also answers to "guarulhos", "cumbica" and "sao paulo". If no name matches, it is a code outside the table and Google can judge it. Otherwise one of those forms has to appear in something you wrote, or the tool refuses and tells the model to ask.

Accepts "business", "premium economy", "primeira classe" and the rest, in a deliberate order: premium is tested first so "premium economy" does not land on economy. An unknown class throws a message listing the four real ones, which is enough for the model to ask you properly.

The three passenger fields, shared by three tools so they cannot drift apart. z.coerce.number() is the small mercy that turns the string "2" into the number 2, because models send strings. Each field has a default and a describe(), and the model reads those descriptions, which is why they are written as instructions.
Builds a filter for flights already in memory, where each of origin, destination and date is optional and an absent one means "any". Returning a function keeps the three analysis tools below short.

The first tool, and one line of work. Its description tells the model it is usually unnecessary, since buscar_voos already accepts city names. Giving the model an easy way to check a city is still worth it: without it, it guesses codes.
Lets the model resolve a date without searching, and it answers with the weekday too, which is what makes "is 12/12 a Saturday?" answerable without a single search.

The main tool. Four gates in two lines: the date must be real and must have been said, and both places must be real and must have been said. Then the search runs for that one day, the results are grouped per leg and summarised, and the warnings are appended. The description is written for the model: one call per leg, and a multi-airport city is searched in full.

A range of consecutive days. Both ends are validated, then line 344 builds the date list with a loop that stops at seven. Line 347 keeps only the cheapest flight per day, line 348 formats one line per day including the weekday, and line 349 says so when the range was cut short rather than silently answering a different question. The description sends the model to buscar_voos for separate days, since this tool would search everything in between.

A calculator, whose existence is the point: the analysis agent is told never to compute in its head. Four operations, reduce over the values, and the Number.isFinite check that turns division by zero into an error instead of Infinity. Rounding to two decimals keeps the result in money shape. The checker also reads the "Resultado:" line this returns, so a legitimate sum is recognised as a fact.
Which legs are in memory and how many flights each has. A cheap tool that stops the model searching again just to find out what it already has.

The busiest analysis tool. Lines 402 to 407 are the four sort orders. Lines 411 and 412 handle a specific weak-model habit worth knowing: models fill unused numeric fields with 0, and here 0 means "non-stop only", so the filter is ignored unless your last message actually mentioned stops, tested with one regex across several languages. Without those two lines, half the filtered answers would quietly show only direct flights.

The filters, in a chain. The falsy checks mean 0 reads as "no limit" for price and duration, since a price limit of zero is not a real request. The airline filter compares unaccented substrings, so "latam" matches "LATAM + Iberia". The departure window compares "HH:MM" strings directly, which works because they are zero-padded. Then the chosen sort.

The output. A clear "nothing passes this filter" is its own answer. Otherwise ten lines, and if there were more, the most expensive flight is named explicitly, because the comment records the real error: without that line the model called the tenth row the most expensive of all. The buy link of the best match is attached.

The schema, which is also the documentation the model reads. Everything is optional except the sort order, which defaults to price, and the two time fields describe their format because a model will otherwise send "8pm". The description lists the four common jobs by name, which is what makes the model pick this tool instead of searching again.

The per-leg summary plus the single cheapest across all legs. That last line is what makes "which airport is cheaper" and "which day is cheaper" answerable in one call, and it is why the description mentions comparing airports and dates.

Round trip totals. Line 468 names which half is missing rather than failing vaguely, so the model knows to search the return. Line 470 pairs every outbound with every return that is not earlier, which is also what makes a return-before-outbound request produce nothing to add up. Then the cheapest total and the best total by cost-benefit. The closing sentence on line 475 is an honesty note that survives into your answer: these are two one-way tickets added together, and buying them as a round trip may cost something else.
Parsing "12h50" into minutes, and a tool that reports the gap between two durations. It exists so the model never subtracts times itself, which is exactly the arithmetic it is worst at.

For a watch, the cheapest flight across every airport pair. It counts successes and keeps the last error, and line 519 only throws when every single search failed. That distinction is what the watcher depends on: a partial failure still produces a usable price instead of a warning.

The route fields of a watch as their own type, so precoAtual can be called both with a database row and with a freshly built object. It splits the comma-separated codes, prices the outbound, prices the return when there is one, and returns null when either leg has no flights. The comment on line 525 draws the line the watcher is built on: null means "no flights", an exception means "could not find out", and those lead to different behaviour.
The one-line description of a watch, used in the tool answers and in the Slack alerts, so both read the same way. Line 541 caps watches at ten, because each one becomes several Google searches a day.

The most careful tool in the file. The limit is checked first, then both dates are validated through the same gate as a search, and a return before the outbound is refused with an instruction to ask rather than to guess.

Building the record, with the places and the class validated on the way in, so nothing invalid can reach the database. Line 560 then re-checks that origin and destination do not overlap after resolution, which is what catches "São Paulo to Congonhas": two different names pointing at the same airport.

The first check happens immediately, which proves the route exists and shows you today's price rather than promising an alert for a route that returns nothing. Lines 564 and 565 work out whether it is already below your target. The insert seeds menor_preco with today's total, and sets avisado_preco only when it is already good, with the comment explaining why: this very answer is the alert, so a second one would be noise.

The reply, assembled from three parts: today's price or "no flights right now", the rule that will trigger an alert, and the buy links. It ends with the honest limit that it only checks while the bot is running, which the writer's rule 9 also enforces. The schema makes data_volta and preco_alvo optional and tells the model to leave them out rather than invent them.
Listing the active watches with their numbers, targets and lowest price seen. The numbers are what the cancel tool takes, which is why the agent instructions say to list before cancelling.

Cancelling by number, and a miss becomes an error pointing the model at the listing tool. The ownership check is not here: harness/dados.ts scopes the update to the conversation, so one channel cannot cancel another channel's watch even if the number is right.

Storing a preference, with two guards. The twenty item cap, and line 627, which refuses any text containing a price. The comment says exactly why: a price stored as a preference would come back as a fact in every later conversation, and the checker would have no way to know it was never searched. The text is also cut to 200 characters.
Listing the stored preferences with their numbers, which is both how you see them and how the model gets the number it needs to delete one.
Deleting a preference by number, with the same error-as-instruction style: a wrong number sends the model to the listing tool instead of failing the request.

The menu: four arrays, one per agent, matching the four entries in harness/agentes.ts. The comment states the rule behind the whole team design: each group belongs to one agent, because fewer options means less confusion. todasAsFerramentas only exists for teste.ts, which uses it to check that no tool ended up in two groups.

Drops arguments whose value is null or an empty string, because weak models send those for optional fields and the code should treat them as absent. harness/agente.ts runs every call's arguments through this before Zod sees them, which turns a whole class of model mistakes into a non-event.
